title: Further Learning: Indigenous Long Island
summary: A starting point for books, Native-authored resources, museums, cultural centers, and continued learning.
content:
Questions visitors ask

Open a question for a concise answer, context, and sources.

What should someone read, visit, or listen to next to learn more about Indigenous Long Island?

To learn more, read John A. Strong’s We Are Still Here! and Gaynell Stone’s Readings in Long Island Archaeology and Ethnohistory series. Visit the Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum and support contemporary Native-led arts at Ma’s House.

To learn about contemporary Indigenous life, read John A. Strong's 'We Are Still Here!' The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today or his deeper histories, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700 and The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island. A vital multi-volume documentary resource is the Suffolk County Archaeological Association's (SCAA) Readings in Long Island Archaeology and Ethnohistory series edited by Gaynell Stone, including Volumes III, IV, and VI. Emic, Native-authored accounts—such as Samson Occom’s 1761 An Account of the Montauk Indians and Unkechaug Chief Lone Otter's (Donald Treadwell) My People, the Unkechaug—offer essential Indigenous-narrated perspectives. For direct support and physical visits, prioritize the Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum and Ma's House & BIPOC Art Studio. older histories by Silas Wood (1826), Benjamin Thompson (1838), and Paul Bailey (1959) contain useful archival material, but should be read with critical awareness of their paternalistic terminology, structural biases, and tendency to promote incorrect 'extinction' or 'vanishing Indian' myths.

Sources

  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here, pp. 6-7, 122.
  • John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700, pp. 20-21, 32.
  • John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island (2001), pp. xiii, 184.
  • Gaynell Stone, The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History (1983), pp. 11-13, 20-21.
  • Gaynell Stone, The History and Archaeology of the Montauk (1993), pp. xiv, 151, 601.
why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
